title: Teaching Large Classes

pts: In large classes, individual attention comes through smart task design, not through individual teacher time per learner.
A well-designed pair task gives every learner simultaneous individual practice, unlike whole-class turn-taking.
The teacher's role shifts from direct deliverer to designer of tasks that scale.

v: Board; a short list of questions

items: Write five questions on the board.
Instead of asking one learner at a time, tell learners to turn to their bench partner and ask and answer all five.
Give three minutes. Walk the aisles listening.
Then ask two or three pairs to share one answer each with the class.
Point out: in three minutes, every learner answered five questions.
Written version: every learner writes an answer on a slate or paper and holds it up.
‘Think, pair, share’ for harder questions.
Support: provide sentence starters on the board.
Stretch: pairs add a follow-up question.

lines: Teacher asks individuals: about 10 learners speak once each.
Pairs: all 60 learners speak many times each.

points.h: Choral and Pair Techniques Scale Best
pts: Choral drilling and pair work let every learner produce language simultaneously, unlike sequential individual turns.
A class of sixty doing pair work generates thirty times more individual speaking practice than the same class taking turns.
This single shift often does more for large-class speaking practice than any other change.

items: Model a short dialogue line.
Whole class repeats.
Half the class says line A; the other half says line B.
Rows or benches take turns.
Pairs practise the whole dialogue.
One or two pairs perform.
‘Disappearing dialogue’: erase words gradually as the class repeats.
Change voice: whisper, loudly, sadly, excitedly.
Support: keep the text visible longer.
Stretch: pairs change one detail and perform a new version.

lines: A: Excuse me, where is the bus stop?

blocks.x: Erase bus stop, then temple, then next to, until learners say the whole dialogue from memory.

points.h: Clear Systems for Noise and Movement
pts: Establish clear routines for transitioning between groupings quickly and quietly, especially in large rooms.
Without a trained routine, large-class transitions consume disproportionate lesson time in noise and confusion.
Practise the routine itself in early lessons until it becomes automatic, freeing later lesson time for content.

v: 5 minutes a lesson for two weeks
A signal (a raised hand, a bell, a clap pattern)

items: Choose one attention signal and teach it: when the teacher raises a hand, learners raise theirs and stop talking.
Practise it several times in the first lessons, timing how long it takes.
Establish routines for handing out and collecting materials (by bench, row leaders).
Establish a routine for moving into groups (bench pairs turn round).
Praise the class when routines get faster.
Use a class ‘noise meter’ drawn on the board.
Appoint rotating row leaders.
Not applicable (whole-class routine).

lines: Benches 1 and 2, turn round and make a group of four.

blocks.x: Timing the signal: day 1, 25 seconds; day 5, 8 seconds; day 10, 4 seconds.

A movable arrow points to the level expected for the current activity. Style: bold, simple. Board version: four bands drawn in chalk.

pts: Train learners to monitor each other's task completion, extending the teacher's limited monitoring capacity.
Assigning a rotating 'group checker' role distributes responsibility without requiring extra teacher time.
This connects to the peer-correction stage of Unit 8's hierarchy, applied at group scale.

items: In each group of four to six, appoint one checker (rotate weekly).
Give checkers the answer key or a checklist for the task.
Checkers confirm the group has completed the task and mark any answers that need attention.
Checkers report to the teacher: ‘Group 5 finished; two questions to check.’
The teacher visits groups that need help.
Checkers check speaking tasks with a simple tick list (did everyone speak?).
Support: checkers are trained first with the teacher.
Stretch: checkers explain answers to their group.

lines: 1. Did everyone finish? 2. Check answers with the key. 3. Circle any wrong answers. 4. Tell the teacher which numbers were hard.

body: Purpose: to show distributed monitoring. Content: a classroom plan with twelve groups, each with one learner wearing a small badge labelled ‘checker’. Arrows from several checkers lead to the teacher, who is visiting two groups marked with a flag. Style: clear plan view. Board version: not applicable.

items: Google Forms (free). Checkers report group results on one shared device.

blocks.x: Checker badges made from card; answer keys on paper.

pts: Supplement spoken instructions with board or handout instructions so understanding doesn't depend on everyone hearing clearly.
In a large room, instructions given only once, only orally, reliably fail to reach a portion of the class.
This is a small addition to Unit 7's instruction-giving that pays off disproportionately at scale.

items: Before any activity, write the instructions on the board in numbered steps.
Say the instructions, pointing to each step.
Demonstrate with learners at the front where everyone can see.
Leave the instructions on the board for the whole activity.
Ask row leaders to check that their rows understood.
Use icons beside instructions for young learners.
For long instructions, give a printed card per bench.
Support: key instruction words in the home language.
Stretch: learners explain instructions to their row.

lines: 1. [two people] Work in pairs. 2. [book] Read the text. 3. [pencil] Answer questions 1–5. 4. [clock] 10 minutes.

body: Purpose: to show legible visual instructions. Content: a board seen from the back of a large classroom, with four large numbered instructions and icons, clearly legible. Style: realistic perspective, clear. Board version: as described.

items: Projector with slides where available; keep instructions on screen throughout the task.

blocks.x: Large, clear writing on the board; test legibility from the back row once.

pts: Use peer and self-assessment, from Unit 8's correction hierarchy, to keep large-class feedback sustainable for the teacher.
Selective marking — checking a rotating sample of work closely rather than everything, every time — preserves feedback quality without unsustainable workload.
A feedback system that isn't sustainable for the teacher eventually collapses into no feedback at all.

items: For objective tasks, learners mark their own or a partner’s work in class using an answer key.
For writing, use a short rubric (three criteria) and mark only one criterion per piece.
Mark a rotating sample of notebooks each week (for example, one row per day).
Give group feedback on common errors rather than individual comments on everything.
Keep a record so every learner receives individual feedback over a fortnight.
Peer marking with a rubric, followed by teacher spot-checks.
Not applicable (teacher activity).

lines: Monday: rows 1–2; Tuesday: rows 3–4; Wednesday: rows 5–6; Thursday: rows 7–8; Friday: common-errors lesson.
Each learner’s notebook is marked in detail once every two weeks; all work is self- or peer-checked in class.

body: Purpose: a planning tool. Content: a weekly grid with days across the top and rows of the classroom down the side, with ticks showing which rows are marked in detail on which day, and a ‘whole-class feedback’ column on Friday. Style: clean table. Board version: not applicable.

items: Google Sheets (free). A marking rota and record.

blocks.x: A paper rota inside the register.

body: Marking everything, every time, is the fastest route to exhaustion and the slowest route to learning. A learner who gets detailed feedback on one piece every two weeks, and checks the rest with a partner, usually improves more than one who gets a tick on every page.

points.sub: Sample, don't try to cover all
pts: Sample a rotating subset of learners closely each lesson rather than attempting equal, exhaustive attention to all every time.
Over a series of lessons, rotation ensures every learner does receive close attention, just not all in the same class.
Attempting universal monitoring every single lesson usually produces shallow attention to everyone instead.

items: Each lesson, choose five to eight ‘focus learners’ to monitor closely.
Rotate so every learner is a focus learner at least once every two weeks.
Record brief notes on each focus learner.
Use notes to update learner profiles.
Share one positive observation with each focus learner.
Choose focus learners by row.
Not applicable (teacher activity).

lines: 12 Sept: Ravi (row 3). Answered two questions in pairs; used because well; still says he go. Told him his reason was clear.

blocks.x: A notebook with one page per learner, or a class list with a notes column.

pts: Resist the pull toward teacher-fronted lecture as the 'only' workable mode for a large class.
Communicative techniques scale with the right structural adjustments — they are not inherently a small-class luxury.
The techniques on this poster are exactly those adjustments, not a compromise on communicative principles.

items: Plan the topic as a short input (8–10 minutes) rather than a full period of talk.
Pause twice for a ‘turn and talk’: learners discuss a question with neighbours for one minute.
Take two or three quick answers from different parts of the room.
End with a one-minute writing task: ‘The most important idea today was…’
Collect a sample of the one-minute papers.
‘Numbered heads’: groups discuss; the teacher calls a number and that learner answers for the group.
Support: provide a partly completed note sheet.
Stretch: learners write a question for the next lesson.

lines: Tell your neighbour one example of this from your own town.
Which of these two ideas do you agree with more? Why?

blocks.x: A large class is not a lecture by necessity; it becomes one by habit (Hess 2001).

body: In your largest class, time how many minutes you speak in one lesson. Next time, add two one-minute ‘turn and talk’ pauses. Count how many learners speak during those two minutes. Most teachers find the number is higher than in the whole of the previous lesson.

dek: Unit 17 of 100: the core techniques from earlier posters still work in large classes — but only with systems that scale attention, monitoring and feedback beyond one teacher's reach.

aims.x: This unit is for teachers of large classes: forty, sixty, a hundred learners or more. It shows how communicative techniques can be adapted to scale, and how systems for talk, movement, monitoring and marking make a large class manageable and productive.
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: create individual practice for every learner through task design;
use choral and pair techniques that scale;
establish routines for noise and movement;
train learners to monitor each other;
give instructions that reach everyone;
keep marking sustainable;
monitor selectively and fairly over time;
resist the pull towards lecturing.

why: Why this matters. In many teaching contexts worldwide, 'large class' is simply what a class is. Techniques designed only for small groups leave most of the world's classrooms unserved.

background.x: Large classes are the everyday reality for millions of English teachers. In many Indian government schools, classes of fifty or sixty are common, and higher numbers are not unusual. Yet much published methodology assumes groups of fifteen or twenty. Teachers of large classes are often left to adapt on their own, or to conclude that communicative teaching is impossible for them.

It is not impossible, but it needs different techniques. Research on large classes, including the Lancaster–Leeds project of the 1980s and more recent work collected by Kuchah Kuchah and Fauzia Shamim (2018), suggests that the main challenges are not purely about numbers. They include noise, space, fixed furniture, lack of materials, marking load and the difficulty of knowing every learner. Each of these has practical responses.

The most important shift is in how a teacher thinks about attention. In a small class, individual attention can mean the teacher speaking to each learner. In a class of sixty, that is arithmetically impossible: even two minutes each would take two hours. Individual attention in a large class comes instead from tasks that give every learner something to do simultaneously, and from systems that let learners support and check one another. A pair task in a class of sixty gives thirty people a turn to speak at the same moment.

items: Participation spread. Use focus-learner notes to confirm every learner has been observed at least once a fortnight.
Routine efficiency. Time the attention signal and group formation weekly.
Peer-checked accuracy. Spot-check peer-marked work to ensure it is reliable.
One-minute papers. Read a sample for understanding of key ideas.
What do you do differently in your largest class compared with your smallest?
How many learners speak in a typical lesson? How could more speak?
How much of your time goes on marking? What would a sustainable system look like?
Which learners in your large classes do you rarely notice? How could you change that?
What would you need to try one new technique from this unit tomorrow?

terms.def: An agreed, taught cue, such as a raised hand or a clap pattern, that tells learners to stop and listen, helping a teacher regain attention quickly in a large class.
Repetition of a word, phrase or sentence by the whole class together after the teacher’s model; useful for pronunciation practice and for building confidence in large classes.
A small group of learners, perhaps five to eight, whom the teacher monitors closely in a given lesson, rotating so that every learner is observed regularly, even in a class of fifty.

A class whose size makes individual attention, movement and marking difficult; in many Indian government schools this means forty to sixty or more learners on fixed benches, calling for routines such as pair work, row leaders and peer checking.

A planned schedule in which the teacher marks different groups or rows of learners’ work in detail on different days, so that every notebook receives careful feedback over a cycle without overwhelming the teacher.
A visual scale, often drawn on the board, that shows the acceptable noise level for an activity and lets the teacher signal when a large class needs to be quieter.
A quick end-of-lesson writing task in which learners note, in about a minute, the most important idea they learnt or a question they still have, giving the teacher rapid feedback.
In a large class, a learner assigned to check a partner’s or row’s work against a model answer, which reduces the teacher’s marking load.

A cooperative structure in which learners think about a question individually, discuss it with a partner and then share ideas with the class (Lyman 1981). It increases participation and gives learners time to prepare.
A quick routine in which learners turn to a neighbour and discuss a question for a minute or two. It gives everyone a chance to speak, even in large classes with fixed benches.
